profile.name: Jumpstyle
profile.tagline: Energetic European electronic dance and music style with fast kicks and jumps
profile.insight: In 2007, Scooter's album 'Jumping All Over the World' topped the UK charts, spotlighting jumpstyle internationally.
profile.profile: Jumpstyle is an electronic dance music genre and dance style originating in Belgium and the Netherlands in the late 1990s. The music features 140–160 BPM tempos with four-on-the-floor 909 kick drums and melodic hardstyle influences. The dance, called jumpen, emphasizes energetic jumps, fast kicks, and rotational footwork, performed mainly with stiff upper bodies and expressive leg movements. Variants include oldschool, hardjump, ownstyle, and freestyle, with competitions often held online and in Europe.
profile.profile_long:
Jumpstyle emerged in Western Europe, particularly Belgium and the Netherlands, in the late 1990s as a subgenre of electronic dance music within the broader hard dance scene. Early influences include Chicago hard house and rave styles, with Belgian artists like Da Boy Tommy popularizing the term around 1997–1998. The genre developed through the early 2000s in Germany and the Netherlands, reaching a commercial peak between 2006 and 2008. Notable musical acts such as Jeckyll & Hyde and Scooter brought jumpstyle to international attention, with Scooter's 2007 album 'Jumping All Over the World' reaching number one on the UK Albums Chart. The music typically features tempos from 140 to 160 BPM, a four-on-the-floor 909 kick drum rhythm, and melodic elements from hardstyle, including pitched basslines and square wave synthesizers.

The dance style, known as jumpen, involves energetic jumps, fast kicks, and rotational footwork synchronized to the music's rhythm. Dancers maintain a relatively stiff upper body, focusing expressive movement in the legs. Several stylistic variants exist: oldschool features simple, fast steps; hardjump introduces six-touch basic steps with a faster tempo; sidejump emphasizes rotations and speed but is less popular; hardfreestyle blends hardjump and sidejump elements; ownstyle, originating in Poland around 2007–2009, is the most popular and innovative variant, incorporating influences from hip-hop and ballet with complex transitions and spins. Tekstyle is a less common style with high kicks and a distinct rhythm.

Jumpstyle dance is performed solo or in groups, with formations such as duo-jump (side-by-side synchronized steps) and duo-kick (facing each other, tapping feet). Group jumps and freestyle sessions are common, with competitions held online and in venues across Europe and Russia. Online communities and social media platforms like TikTok have helped sustain and revive jumpstyle, including the emergence of the microgenre yabujin-core pioneered by Lithuanian rapper Yabujin.

Costumes are typically casual streetwear suitable for energetic movement, with no sacred or restricted elements. Events and clubs in Belgium and other European countries regularly host jumpstyle parties and competitions. Notable figures include Patrick Jumpen, Scot, and Jagr, who have contributed to the dance's popularity through performances and online tutorials. Jumpstyle shares lineage with gabber, hardstyle, and techno hardcore, and its dance style is sometimes compared to the Dutch hakken dance but with more aerial jumps and kicks. Despite a decline in mainstream popularity after the 2000s, jumpstyle remains a living tradition with active communities worldwide.

sections.origins_and_history: Jumpstyle originated in Belgium in the late 1990s, around 1997–1998, with early contributions from artists like Da Boy Tommy. It developed further in the Netherlands and Germany in the early 2000s. The genre peaked commercially between 2006 and 2008, with hits by Jeckyll & Hyde and Scooter's international success. After a decline in mainstream presence in the 2010s, jumpstyle sustained a dedicated following online and experienced a revival in the 2020s through the yabujin-core microgenre.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Jumpstyle dance, called jumpen, involves energetic jumps, fast kicks, and rotational footwork timed to the music. Dancers keep a stiff upper body and focus movement in their legs. Variants include oldschool (simple 5-touch steps), hardjump (6-touch steps with faster tempo), sidejump (more rotations, less popular), hardfreestyle (blend of hardjump and sidejump), and ownstyle (innovative, incorporating spins and influences from hip-hop and ballet). Dances can be solo or in groups, with duo-jump (side-by-side synchronized steps) and duo-kick (facing and tapping feet).
sections.music_and_instruments: Jumpstyle music features tempos between 140 and 160 BPM, a four-on-the-floor 909 kick drum rhythm, and melodic elements from hardstyle such as pitched basslines and square wave synthesizers. It developed from tech-trance, hardstyle, gabber, and makina. The sound is characterized by short, semi-distorted kicks and a minimal melodic arrangement. Later productions incorporated electro house influences.
sections.costume_and_setting: Jumpstyle dancers typically wear casual streetwear suitable for vigorous leg movements and jumps. Events take place in clubs, festivals, and public spaces across Europe, with notable venues in Belgium such as Complexe Cap'tain and Pulse Factory. Social media and online platforms also serve as venues for competitions and community gatherings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Jumpstyle is danced socially at clubs, festivals, and competitions. It is a non-sacred, secular dance form associated with electronic music culture. Competitions occur both online and in person, including European Jump Masters and World Sidejump League. The dance fosters community and individual expression through its variants and freestyle elements.
sections.notable_figures: Patrick Jumpen is a seminal figure in jumpstyle dance and music, known for popularizing the dance and producing tutorials. DJs and producers like Da Boy Tommy, Jeckyll & Hyde, Scooter, and Lithuanian rapper Yabujin have been influential in the music scene. Prominent dancers include Scot, Jagr, and Vedr from Serbia.
sections.regional_variants: Variants of jumpstyle dance include oldschool, hardjump, sidejump, hardfreestyle, ownstyle, and tekstyle. Ownstyle, originating in Poland around 2007–2009, is the most popular worldwide. Regional differences affect dance speed, style, and incorporation of other dance influences, with Eastern Europe favoring more aerial jumps and Southern Europe emphasizing grounded movements.
sections.lineage: Jumpstyle descends from European hard dance genres such as gabber, hardstyle, tech-trance, and makina, with early influences from Chicago hard house. It shares musical and dance characteristics with gabber and hardstyle but is distinct in tempo and style. The dance is related to Dutch hakken but features more jumps and kicks.

basic_steps: Stand with feet together, knees slightly bent
Jump and kick right foot forward while left foot stays grounded
Jump and switch feet, left foot forward, right foot grounded
Add rotational footwork by pivoting on supporting foot
Incorporate arm movements for balance, keeping upper body stiff

teaching.formation: Solo, duo (side-by-side or facing), or group synchronized dancing

The sound is minimal yet energetic, with rhythmic offbeats and melodic elements drawn from hardstyle and techno hardcore.

movement_profile.posture: Relatively stiff upper body with slight knee bend for jumps
movement_profile.footwork: Alternating kicks forward with feet, rotational pivots on supporting foot, fast jumps timed to beat
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Used mainly for balance, generally kept controlled and close to body
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Minimal torso movement, hips follow leg kicks subtly
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Danced solo, duo side-by-side or facing, or in synchronized groups
movement_profile.partnering: Duo-kick involves facing partner and tapping feet; physical contact otherwise avoided
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Energetic, fast-paced with precise timing to 140–160 BPM music
